title: Contract-driven client simulator and compatibility test specification
author: Liam Chen
content:
Summary:

This specification defines a contract-driven client simulator and compatibility test harness for Redwood Inference SDKs and internal clients. The goal is to detect regressions in client behavior against authoritative API contracts before they reach downstream consumers (hosted API, Dedicated, Private). The approach combines lightweight API contract manifests, a deterministic request/response simulator, and a compatibility matrix that runs as part of CI and periodic nightly validation.

Goals:
- Provide a single, repeatable executable that validates SDKs and internal client libraries against the current API contract.
- Detect breaking changes (semantic or structural) in request schema, streaming semantics, error taxonomy, and retry/timeout behavior.
- Exercise runtime behaviors (streaming, chunk reassembly, partial result resume) via deterministic simulations.
- Produce human-friendly failure reports and machine-readable artifacts for automated triage.

Scope and Non-Goals:
- In scope: JSON/HTTP contract checks, streaming protocol simulations (chunked JSON), idempotency semantics, error-code mapping, retry guidance adherence, and client-side instrumentation hooks.
- Out of scope: full production load testing, model output quality evaluation, tenant billing reconciliation. Those are handled by dedicated performance and billing suites.

Background and Motivation:
Redwood maintains multiple SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java) and an internal edge client used by routing/proxy layers. Historically, compatibility regressions surfaced in downstream services weeks after deploy — typically when clients misinterpreted a streaming boundary, an optional field became mandatory, or error codes changed. A contract-first simulator reduces this feedback loop by shifting detection left into CI and scheduled validation jobs.

High-level design:
1) Contract manifest (YAML): authoritative description of endpoints, request/response schemas (JSON Schema), streaming semantics, and stability annotations (stable/experimental/deprecated). Each manifest is versioned alongside service API and published to the contract registry (git + signed release).
2) Simulator engine: deterministic runtime that consumes the manifest and runs a series of scripted scenarios. Scenarios include nominal flows, partial-stream interruptions, injected latency/jitter, and common error cases. The simulator can run in:
   - unit mode (fast, single scenario),
   - CI mode (parallelized across matrix cells), and
   - nightly mode (exhaustive scenarios across SDKs and model variants).
3) Client adapters: thin wrappers per SDK that translate simulated transport events into SDK-level calls and capture client outputs, logs, and metrics.
4) Compatibility matrix: per-SDK matrix of pass/fail, semantic diffs, and a severity score. Matrix feeds Slack/PR checks and a Confluence dashboard.

Contract Manifest (required fields):
- service: short name (string)
- version: semver (string)
- endpoints: list of endpoint objects with:
  - path (string), method (string), id (string)
  - request_schema (JSON Schema document or reference)
  - response_schema (JSON Schema document or reference)
  - streaming: none | chunked-json | server-sent | bidi
  - streaming_checkpointing: supports_resume | no_resume | partial_resume
  - stability: stable | experimental | deprecated
  - allowed_error_codes: list of numeric codes and reason strings

Example manifest snippet (YAML) included in Appendix A. The manifest must live in the contracts/ directory of the API repo and be signed by the owning service.

Simulator Scenarios (examples):
- Nominal: full request, full response, validate JSON schema, validate latency under simulated 50ms RTT.
- Chunk-splitting: simulate chunk boundaries mid-object (verify client reassembly).
- Partial resume: simulate truncated stream and then resume from last checkpoint token sequence. Ensure SDK reconstructs final result when resume succeeds.
- Error injection: inject 429 with Retry-After, 503 transient with exponential backoff observation; verify client backoff and retry counters.
- Schema drift: server emits extra optional fields or missing optional fields; simulator records non-fatal vs fatal validation outcomes per stability annotation.

Severity scoring rules (how failures escalate):
- Score 5 (Critical): Required field missing in response, streaming boundary loss leading to corrupt application-level payload, or change in idempotency semantics that could cause duplication. Immediate release-blocking in mainline CI.
- Score 4 (Major): Error code remapping or missing documented error that changes retry behavior. Fails gating for patch releases.
- Score 3 (Medium): Optional field appears/disappears for stable endpoints. Tracked in SDK backlog but not blocking.
- Score 2 (Minor): Cosmetic changes in field names under experimental endpoints.
- Score 1 (Info): Telemetry/metadata additions not referenced by client.

Reporter and artifact format:
- Each run emits a human summary (Markdown) plus machine artifact (NDJSON) with one event per scenario. Artifact fields: scenario_id, sdk, endpoint_id, outcome, observed_payload_hash, diff_summary, severity_score, timestamp. Artifacts are published to object storage with predictable path: s3://redwood-contracts/{manifest_version}/{sdk}/{run_timestamp}/results.ndjson

CI integration and gating policy:
- Pull Request checks: unit-mode simulator runs per PR for the changed SDK module and endpoint. PR must pass all Score >=4 checks before merging to release branches.
- Nightly validation: full matrix runs nightly; failed Score >=3 scenarios open automated tickets in the service team backlog and notify owners.
- Release validation: before any API minor/major bump, run exhaustive compatibility matrix; release blocked on unresolved critical Score 5 failures.

Runtime behavior checks (list of concrete assertions simulator enforces):
- JSON schema conformance (strict for stable endpoints).
- Streaming checkpoint token monotonicity for resumeable streams.
- Idempotency key handling: server-simulated dedup semantics must result in idempotent client semantics when key present.
- Retry/backoff: client must follow Retry-After and not exceed configured retry budget (default 4 retries, exponential backoff with jitter).
- Timeout propagation: SDKs must expose and propagate context cancellation within 50ms of cancel event in the simulation.

Observability and telemetry hooks:
- Simulator emits spans with service=contract-sim, scenario, sdk, endpoint tags.
- SDK adapters must surface a lightweight test-only hook that returns captured request/response traces and token-level timing for the simulator to assert on.
- All runs tagged with manifest_version for traceability.

Failure handling and triage playbook (runbook steps):
1) Check the NDJSON artifact to identify failing scenario_id and severity_score.
2) Reproduce locally using the simulator binary with --scenario <id> and the SDK under test.
3) Inspect captured traces and the diff_summary. If schema mismatch, check manifest version and service changelog.
4) If change is intentional (service owner confirms), update SDK compatibility shim documented in sdk-compat/ and open a cross-repo change with the service.
5) If unintentional, roll back client change or apply fast-fix and run the CI-mode simulator.

Adoption and rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (Q4 2025): implement simulator core, Python and TS adapters, run in SDK PR checks.
- Phase 2 (Q1 2026): add Go/Java adapters, nightly matrix, Confluence dashboard, and Slack alerts.
- Phase 3 (Q2 2026): require release-gate for API minor/major changes and integrate with contract registry signing.

Ownership and KPIs:
- Owners: Runtime QA (primary), SDK platform (secondary), API product (stakeholder).
- KPIs: mean time to detect compatibility failure (target: < 1 hour for PR checks, < 24 hours for nightly), number of post-release regressions attributable to client compatibility (target: 0 per quarter), percentage PRs blocked due to uncovered compatibility failures (target: 2% or lower).

Security and data handling:
- No customer data should be present in contract manifests or simulator payloads. Use synthetic prompt templates and redaction rules.
- Artifacts with potential PII must be automatically scrubbed before publishing to object storage.

Appendix A — example contract manifest snippet (YAML):
```yaml
service: text-generation
version: 1.8.0
endpoints:
  - id: generate-stream
    path: /v1/generate
    method: POST
    request_schema: ./schemas/generate.request.json
    response_schema: ./schemas/generate.response.json
    streaming: chunked-json
    streaming_checkpointing: supports_resume
    stability: stable
    allowed_error_codes:
      - code: 429
        reason: rate_limit
      - code: 503
        reason: transient_error
```

Appendix B — example CLI usage (simulator):
- Run single scenario: ./contract-sim --manifest contracts/text-generation-1.8.0.yaml --sdk python --scenario generate-stream-nominal
- Run CI matrix: ./contract-sim --manifest contracts/text-generation-1.8.0.yaml --matrix ci.yaml --output results.ndjson

Appendix C — sample failure message (Markdown):
- Title: generate-stream: chunk-splitting failed (Score 5)
- Summary: SDK failed to reassemble JSON object when server split chunk inside a nested array. Observed: malformed JSON at byte 245.
- Steps to reproduce: link to runnable artifact and command line.
- Suggested owners: sdk-python-team, service-text-generation.

Open questions and future work:
- How to integrate model-variant non-determinism into the simulation without producing false positives? Proposed approach: separate semantic checks (schema + framing) from content checks and allow an opt-in quality evaluation layer.
- Can we reuse the simulator to exercise private deployment runtime differences (VPC/private proxy behaviors)? Proposed: add a private-deploy adapter that mimics proxy timeouts and auth differences.
